title: Session login endpoint with per-username lockout and bounded verification work

source_request.text:
Add session login to the toy service: POST /login with JSON {username, password}. Valid credentials of a registered user return 200 with a random session token; wrong password or unknown user return 401 with the same generic error body; after 5 failed attempts for one username within 60 seconds further attempts return 429 until the window passes; passwords and tokens are never written to logs. Add focused tests.
Also bound the total password-verification work server-wide: at most 4 password verifications may run at the same time and at most 16 more may wait; a login request beyond that gets 503 with a Retry-After header and the same generic error body, and is not counted as a failed attempt for its username.

coverage.excerpt: Add session login to the toy service: POST /login with JSON {username, password}.
Valid credentials of a registered user return 200 with a random session token
wrong password or unknown user return 401 with the same generic error body
after 5 failed attempts for one username within 60 seconds further attempts return 429 until the window passes
passwords and tokens are never written to logs
Also bound the total password-verification work server-wide: at most 4 password verifications may run at the same time and at most 16 more may wait
a login request beyond that gets 503 with a Retry-After header and the same generic error body
and is not counted as a failed attempt for its username.

product.problem: The toy service (src/server.js) only serves GET /health; the in-memory fake user store in src/users.js can verify a password (users.verify) but nothing exposes it. Clients have no way to exchange a registered user's credentials for a session token, and an exposed check would need a guard against password guessing, a response that does not reveal which usernames exist, and a guarantee that secrets never reach the logs (CLAUDE.md: "never log passwords"). Password verification is expensive: users.verify and hashPassword run crypto.scryptSync, which blocks the event loop for every call, and nothing bounds how much of that work many concurrent login requests can start at once.
actors: HTTP client of the toy service logging in as a registered synthetic user (alice or bob from test/fixtures/users.js)
Unauthenticated caller who may send wrong passwords or unknown usernames, including an attacker guessing passwords
Operator who reads the service output (stdout/stderr) and must never see passwords or tokens there
Many concurrent callers (legitimate or a flood) whose combined login traffic must not start unbounded password-verification work on the server

goals.statement: A registered user can POST valid credentials as JSON to /login and receive a fresh random session token.
A failed login does not reveal whether the username exists: wrong password and unknown user get the same 401 response.

Password guessing against one username is bounded to at most 5 failed attempts in any 60-second span, also under concurrent requests: once a username has 5 failures within the last 60 seconds it gets 429 until the oldest of those 5 failures is 60 seconds old.
Passwords and session tokens are never written to the service logs.
The login behaviour is pinned by focused tests that run under npm test, and the existing GET /health and 404 behaviour keeps working.

Total password-verification work is bounded per server: at most 4 verifications run at the same time and at most 16 more wait; a login request beyond that is refused at once with 503, a Retry-After header and the generic error body, and does not count as a failed attempt for its username.

non_goals.statement: Using the token on other endpoints: no endpoint validates or consumes the token, and there is no logout, refresh or token expiry.
non_goals.rationale: The request asks only for issuing a token at login; no existing route needs authentication.

non_goals.statement: User registration, password changes or persistent storage of users or sessions.
non_goals.rationale: src/users.js is a local in-memory fake store built from synthetic fixture users (README.md); the request does not ask to change it.

non_goals.statement: Per-IP rate limiting, or a global limit on the number of login attempts per unit of time.
non_goals.rationale: The request limits failures per username and caps concurrent verification work (DEC-010), not the attempt rate per client or overall; see RISK-001 for the accepted gap.

non_goals.statement: Changing the password hashing scheme in src/users.js (scrypt with Node defaults, KEY_LENGTH 32, a random 16-byte salt per user) or the behaviour of its existing exports createUserStore, has, usernames, verify and hashPassword.
non_goals.rationale: users.verify already does a salted scrypt hash with a constant-time comparison; this feature only adds asynchronous twins (store.verifyAsync and the exported hashPasswordAsync, DEC-011) with identical parameters so that verification can run off the event loop under the DEC-010 gate.

non_goals.statement: TLS, cookies, CSRF protection or Set-Cookie session handling.
non_goals.rationale: The request specifies a JSON body response with the token; transport security is outside this toy service.

constraints: Zero dependencies: package.json has no dependencies and README.md calls the service dependency-free; use only Node built-ins (node:http, node:crypto).
CLAUDE.md: never log passwords (extended here to tokens by the request).
Tests run with npm test, which is node --test "test/**/*.test.js" (package.json); new tests are node:test files under test/ and use test/helpers.js listen() on an ephemeral 127.0.0.1 port.

src/users.js changes only additively (DEC-011): createUserStore, has, usernames, verify and hashPassword keep their behaviour, so test/users.test.js passes unchanged; test/fixtures/users.js, test/helpers.js and the existing tests stay unchanged.
All new state (failure records, sessions, the verification queue) is in memory, per createServer instance, and bounded.
createServer(options) keeps its current signature and defaults: createServer() with no options must still work (test/health.test.js calls it).
risks: Rate-limit boundary off-by-one (429 on the 5th instead of the 6th attempt, or not at all), a lockout that never ends, or a fixed-window reset that lets a burst of more than 5 failures through at the window boundary; pinned by LOGIN-003 tests with an injected clock. A handler that verifies before checking the lock still answers 429 but defeats INV-003; pinned by LOGIN-003-AC7 call counters.

With asynchronous verification several attempts for one username can be in flight at once; if the lock counted only finished failures, concurrent guesses would exceed 5 per window. Pinned by LOGIN-003-AC9 (in-flight attempts count toward the lock, DEC-003).
User enumeration through a different 401 or 503 body, a 429 that applies only to registered users, or a measurable timing gap; mitigated by DEC-004, DEC-005, DEC-010 and INV-002.
Accidental logging of the request body or token during debugging; pinned by LOGIN-004.

A gate slot that is not released on an error path would shrink capacity until every login gets 503; pinned by LOGIN-007-AC5. An asynchronous hash that differs from the synchronous one would reject every correct password; pinned by LOGIN-007-AC6.
node --test with a missing test file fails, but a renamed test inside a file would not; each proof therefore runs a whole dedicated file rather than a name pattern.
success_metrics: Each of the six focused test files (test/login-success.test.js, test/login-failure.test.js, test/login-ratelimit.test.js, test/login-validation.test.js, test/login-logging.test.js, test/login-concurrency.test.js) exits 0 under node --test.
npm test exits 0 with 0 failing tests, including the 5 existing tests in test/health.test.js and test/users.test.js.
Every isolated_mutation negative control makes its proof command exit nonzero (28 of 28 mutations detected).
In the logging test, 0 captured log writes contain the submitted password or any issued token.

The 6th attempt within 60 seconds after 5 failures returns 429 in 100% of test runs, an attempt made once the oldest of those 5 failures is 60 seconds old returns a normal response, and no 60-second span in the rate-limit tests contains more than 5 401 responses for one username, including 8 concurrent wrong-password requests (exactly 5 reach verification).
Under 10001 insertions, createSessionStore().size() and createFailureLimiter().size() each stay at 10000.

In the concurrency tests the number of verifications in progress never exceeds 4, the queue never holds more than 16, and the 21st concurrent request gets 503 within 2 seconds while no further verification starts.

architecture.approach: Add one new module, src/login.js, holding the login logic, route POST /login to it from src/server.js, and add asynchronous verification twins to src/users.js. src/login.js exports createSessionStore(), createFailureLimiter({ maxFailures, windowMs, maxTracked, now }) and createVerificationGate({ maxActive, maxQueued }) (each option defaulting to the DEC-001 constant, now to Date.now) and createLoginHandler({ users, sessions, limiter, gate }), which returns a (req, res) handler. The handler reads the body up to 4096 bytes, parses and validates {username, password}, asks the limiter whether the username is locked (429), asks the gate for a verification slot (503 with Retry-After and the generic 401 body when 4 verifications run and 16 wait, nothing counted), and, once the slot is granted, reserves the attempt with the limiter (429 if the username became locked meanwhile, DEC-003), awaits users.verifyAsync for a registered username (or an equivalent hashPasswordAsync with a dummy salt for an unknown one), releases the slot, then records a failure and returns 401 on mismatch, or issues a token from the session store and returns 200 {"token": ...} (a success leaves the failure record unchanged). createServer(options) gains optional options.sessions (default createSessionStore()), options.now (default Date.now) and options.gate (default createVerificationGate()) and builds one limiter (createFailureLimiter({ now }), so the limiter uses the default MAX_FAILURES, WINDOW_MS and MAX_TRACKED) and one handler per server instance, so the gate is shared by every request to that server; GET /health and the 404 fallback are unchanged. src/login.js writes its responses with a local sendJson(res, status, body, headers) that sets the same content-type and content-length headers as the sendJson in src/server.js plus any extra header (retry-after, connection), because src/server.js does not export its helper. Tests drive the real HTTP server through test/helpers.js listen() and fetch, with an injected clock for the time window, an injected session store for readback, an injected gate whose active() and queued() they observe, and an injected users object whose verifyAsync is a call-counting spy that either forwards to createUserStore(USERS) or returns promises the test settles; the session-store, limiter and gate bounds are also tested by calling their factories directly.

decisions.decision: New module src/login.js owns body parsing, validation, the failure limiter, the session store, the verification gate and the handler; src/server.js only routes req.method === "POST" && url.pathname === "/login" to the handler and passes options.users, options.sessions, options.now and options.gate. Constants exported from src/login.js: MAX_BODY_BYTES = 4096, MAX_USERNAME_LENGTH = 64, MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH = 1024, MAX_FAILURES = 5, WINDOW_MS = 60000, MAX_TRACKED = 10000, MAX_ACTIVE_VERIFICATIONS = 4, MAX_QUEUED_VERIFICATIONS = 16, BUSY_RETRY_AFTER_S = 1.
decisions.rationale: Keeps src/server.js a thin router like today and gives the login logic one owner that tests can import (createSessionStore, createFailureLimiter, createVerificationGate) with only an additive change to src/users.js (DEC-011).

decisions.decision: A token is crypto.randomBytes(32).toString("base64url") (43 characters, 256 bits). The success response is 200 with body {"token": "<token>"} and nothing else. The session store (createSessionStore) keeps token -> { username, createdAt } in a Map, exposes issue(username) -> token, usernameFor(token) -> username or null, and size(), and holds at most MAX_TRACKED (10000) sessions: when issue() is called while size() is 10000, it first deletes the oldest-issued token (first in Map insertion order), so size() never exceeds 10000 and the evicted token's usernameFor returns null.
decisions.rationale: The request asks for a random session token; a CSPRNG with 256 bits is unguessable, base64url is JSON- and header-safe, and a bounded in-memory store gives the token a server-side meaning that tests can read back without adding any endpoint.

decisions.decision: Failure limiter semantics, per exact username string (registered or not), as a sliding window that also counts attempts in flight. Per username the limiter keeps the timestamps (now() values) of its most recent counted failures, at most 5, and a pending count of attempts currently in verification. Every check first drops timestamps with now() - ts >= 60000 (WINDOW_MS) and deletes the record when no timestamp and no pending attempt remain. The username is locked when timestamps + pending >= 5: the attempt, even with the correct password, returns 429 {"error": "too many attempts"} without verifying the password and without counting, with a Retry-After header of ceil((oldest + 60000 - now()) / 1000) seconds when 5 timestamps remain (oldest is the earliest of them) and of BUSY_RETRY_AFTER_S (1) seconds when the lock is due only to attempts in flight. Otherwise the attempt proceeds; each 401 appends now() (keeping only the newest 5). A successful login does not clear or change the timestamps. Requests rejected with 400, 413 or 503, and verifications that reject (500), never count. API: createFailureLimiter returns { check(username) -> { locked: boolean, retryAfter: whole seconds (0 when not locked) }, begin(username) -> the same result, end(username, failed), recordFailure(username), size() }; check() never creates a record; begin() runs the same test and, when not locked, increments pending (creating the record if needed); end() decrements pending (never below 0) and, when failed is true, calls recordFailure(), which appends now(); size() is the number of tracked usernames. The handler calls check() on arrival, before asking the gate for a slot, and begin() at the start of its gate task, before any users.has, users.verifyAsync or hashPasswordAsync call, returning 429 immediately when either reports locked, and calls end() once the verification settles. Bound: the limiter tracks at most maxTracked (MAX_TRACKED, 10000) usernames; when begin() or recordFailure() would add a new username while size() equals maxTracked, it first deletes every record with no unexpired timestamp and no pending attempt and, if size() is still maxTracked, deletes the record created earliest (first in Map insertion order), so size() never exceeds maxTracked.
decisions.rationale: Implements "after 5 failed attempts for one username within 60 seconds further attempts return 429 until the window passes" literally: a 6th failure can only be counted when fewer than 5 failures lie in the preceding 60 seconds, so no 60-second span ever holds more than 5 401 responses for one username, and the lock lasts until the oldest of the 5 failures is 60 seconds old ("until the window passes"). Because verification is now asynchronous (DEC-011) up to 4 attempts can be in verification at once and up to 16 wait; counting only finished failures would let concurrent guesses for one username pass the check together and produce more than 5 401 responses in a window, so attempts in flight count toward the lock and the lock is re-tested when a queued attempt gets its slot. A fixed window opened at the first failure was rejected because it lets up to 9 failures through within 60 seconds around the window boundary. Clearing the record on success was dropped because the request does not ask for it and it would give an attacker 5 fresh guesses each time the real user logs in; a user who knows the password is not affected while unlocked. Not verifying while locked also bounds scrypt work per username, and storing at most 5 timestamps keeps each record bounded.

decisions.decision: For a username the store does not know (users.has is false), the gate task awaits hashPasswordAsync(password, DUMMY_SALT) from src/users.js, with DUMMY_SALT = crypto.randomBytes(16) created once per module load, discards the result and treats the attempt as a failure; this dummy hash holds a gate slot exactly like a real verification. src/login.js keeps a reference to the src/users.js module object (require("./users.js")) and reads hashPasswordAsync from it at call time, so a test that replaces that export with a counting wrapper before it first requires src/server.js observes every call.
decisions.rationale: users.verifyAsync, like users.verify, resolves false immediately for an unknown user, which would make unknown-user responses measurably faster than wrong-password responses; doing the same scrypt work removes that gross timing signal (residual differences: RISK-004), and running it under the gate keeps it inside the server-wide bound.

decisions.decision: Fixed generic bodies, all with content-type application/json: 401 {"error": "invalid credentials"} for both wrong password and unknown user; 503 the same {"error": "invalid credentials"} body, byte-identical to the 401 body, with retry-after: 1; 429 {"error": "too many attempts"}; 400 {"error": "invalid request"}; 413 {"error": "payload too large"}; 500 {"error": "internal error"} when a verification promise rejects. No response echoes any request field.
decisions.rationale: The request requires the same generic error body for both 401 cases and for the 503 refusal; fixed bodies cannot leak input. A rejected verification (not expected from crypto.scrypt with validated string inputs) must still answer and must not be reported as a credential failure.

decisions.decision: createServer accepts options.now (a function returning milliseconds, default Date.now) and passes it to the limiter, and options.gate (a gate from createVerificationGate, default createVerificationGate()) and passes it to the handler; tests inject a controllable clock instead of sleeping 60 seconds and an observable gate instead of guessing queue state.
decisions.rationale: Makes the window-passes behaviour and the queue bound testable deterministically and fast.

decisions.decision: Any method other than POST on /login falls through to the existing 404 {"error": "not found"} response.
decisions.rationale: Keeps the router's current behaviour for unknown routes; no new method semantics are requested.

decisions.decision: src/login.js and the additions to src/users.js contain no console or process.stdout/stderr calls; the only log line of the service remains "listening on <port>" in src/server.js. Body parse errors are caught and mapped to 400, and verification rejections to 500, without logging or rethrowing.
decisions.rationale: The simplest way to guarantee "passwords and tokens are never written to logs" is to log nothing on the login path.

decisions.decision: The body is read as a Buffer with a running byte count; once it exceeds MAX_BODY_BYTES the handler stops buffering, responds 413 with a connection: close header and discards the rest of the request. Only a parsed JSON object whose username and password are both strings, 1..64 and 1..1024 characters respectively, is accepted; anything else (invalid JSON, an array, null, missing or non-string fields) is 400. The content-type request header is not required.
decisions.rationale: Bounds memory per request and the scrypt input size; strict typing prevents prototype or type confusion reaching users.verify.

decisions.decision: Server-wide verification gate. createVerificationGate({ maxActive = MAX_ACTIVE_VERIFICATIONS (4), maxQueued = MAX_QUEUED_VERIFICATIONS (16) }) returns { run(task), active(), queued() }. run(task): if active() < maxActive it increments active and starts task() at once; else if queued() < maxQueued it appends task to a FIFO queue; else it returns null synchronously and starts nothing. Otherwise it returns a Promise settled with task()'s outcome. When a running task settles (resolve or reject) the gate decrements active in a finally step and starts the oldest queued task. One gate per createServer instance (options.gate) is shared by every POST /login request, and every password-verification unit of work, users.verifyAsync for a registered username and the DEC-004 dummy hashPasswordAsync for an unknown one, runs only as a gate task. The handler asks for a slot after validation and after the arrival check() and before any verification; when run() returns null it answers 503 with retry-after: 1 (BUSY_RETRY_AFTER_S) and the 401 body {"error": "invalid credentials"} and changes no limiter state. The slot is released as soon as the verification settles, before the session is issued and the response is written. A queued request whose client disconnects keeps its place and still runs.
decisions.rationale: Implements "at most 4 password verifications may run at the same time and at most 16 more may wait; a login request beyond that gets 503 with a Retry-After header and the same generic error body, and is not counted as a failed attempt": the 503 is decided before any verification or limiter change, so it neither costs scrypt work nor counts. Counting the dummy hash as a verification makes the bound total, as the request asks ("total password-verification work"), and keeps unknown and registered usernames indistinguishable by queueing behaviour. Retry-After is a constant 1 second because the queue drains in a few scrypt durations and the value must not depend on the username. Releasing the slot in finally keeps a rejected verification from shrinking capacity. Not dropping queued work on client disconnect keeps the gate simple; that work is bounded by maxQueued.

decisions.decision: src/users.js gains, additively, an exported hashPasswordAsync(password, salt) that returns a Promise resolving to the same Buffer as hashPassword(password, salt), computed with crypto.scrypt(password, salt, KEY_LENGTH) (Node defaults, as scryptSync), and a store method verifyAsync(username, password) that resolves false at once for an unknown user or a non-string password and otherwise resolves crypto.timingSafeEqual(await hashPasswordAsync(password, user.salt), user.hash). The existing createUserStore, has, usernames, verify and hashPassword are unchanged. The login handler uses only verifyAsync and hashPasswordAsync.
decisions.rationale: users.verify runs crypto.scryptSync on the event loop, so with it at most one verification could ever be running and the 4-running/16-waiting bound of the request would never engage, while every attempt blocked all other requests. crypto.scrypt runs the same computation on the libuv threadpool (4 threads by default), so the gate bounds real concurrent work and the server stays responsive. The salts and hashes are private to the store closure, so the asynchronous path has to live in src/users.js; keeping the scheme and the existing exports unchanged honours NG-004 and keeps test/users.test.js valid.

decisions.decision: Every runtime proof command and the unit command run node --test with --test-timeout=20000 and --test-force-exit, so a test that waits on a response or a verification that never settles fails after 20 seconds and the process exits nonzero instead of running until the proof timeout.
decisions.rationale: Under an isolated mutation such as removing the queue bound, a request can stay parked forever; the test then fails its assertion but its finally block waits for that response, so a plain node --test never exits and the run ends only at the 120 s proof timeout, which proves nothing. The bounded flags keep each unmutated proof unchanged (it finishes in about a second) and turn such a hang into a plain test failure.

invariants.statement: No password and no issued token is ever written to stdout, stderr or any console method, and no response other than the 200 success body contains a token.
For any username, the 401 response to a wrong password and the 401 response to an unknown user have the same status, the same content-type and byte-identical bodies.

While a username is locked (5 counted failures within the last 60 seconds, or counted failures plus attempts in verification reaching 5), no request for it reaches users.verifyAsync or hashPasswordAsync.

Memory is bounded: a request body is buffered up to 4096 bytes, the limiter tracks at most 10000 usernames, the session store holds at most 10000 tokens, and the verification gate holds at most 16 waiting requests and runs at most 4 scrypt computations (about 16 MiB each at Node's defaults N=16384, r=8).
GET /health and the 404 response for unknown routes behave exactly as before the feature.

Per server instance, at most 4 password verifications (users.verifyAsync or the dummy hashPasswordAsync) are in progress and at most 16 login requests wait for one at any time; a request that finds both full is answered 503 without any verification and without changing its username's failure record, and every finished or rejected verification frees its slot.

components.name: Login module
components.description: src/login.js: body reading with the 4096-byte cap, JSON parsing and validation, the per-username failure limiter (createFailureLimiter), the bounded session store (createSessionStore), the server-wide verification gate (createVerificationGate) and the POST /login handler (createLoginHandler).

components.name: HTTP router
components.description: src/server.js: routes POST /login to the login handler, accepts the optional sessions, now and gate options, keeps GET /health, the 404 fallback and the startup log line unchanged.

components.name: User store
components.description: src/users.js: the existing in-memory fake user store, extended additively with the asynchronous hashPasswordAsync export and the store method verifyAsync (DEC-011); existing exports unchanged.

security.data_exposure: POST /login is unauthenticated and reachable by anyone who can reach the server; that is its purpose. It returns only: on success the token for the user whose credentials were presented ({"token"} and nothing else, no user data); otherwise one of the fixed bodies of DEC-005, none of which echo input. The 401 body is identical for unknown users and wrong passwords, the 503 refusal carries that same body and a constant retry-after: 1 and is decided before the username is looked up, the limiter applies to registered and unknown usernames alike, and an unknown username's dummy hash takes a gate slot like a real verification, so neither the body, the 401/429/503 status nor the Retry-After header tells a caller whether a username exists. The token is a bearer secret returned only in the 200 body to the requester; the server keeps token -> username only in the in-memory session store, which no endpoint exposes (GET /health still returns only the user count). Passwords are never stored (users.js keeps salted scrypt hashes; verifyAsync only compares) and neither passwords nor tokens are logged (INV-001). Authorization scope: a token grants nothing yet (NG-001).
security.input_validation: The only new external input is the POST /login request body. Body: at most 4096 bytes, else 413 and buffering stops (DEC-009). It must parse as JSON into a plain object (not an array or null), else 400. username: required, typeof string, length 1..64 characters, else 400. password: required, typeof string, length 1..1024 characters, else 400. Extra fields are ignored. The username is used only as a Map key and as the users.has/verifyAsync argument; it is never interpolated into output. Invalid requests are rejected before the limiter, before the gate and before any hashing, and do not count as failures. No header, query parameter or cookie is read. The new createServer options (sessions, now, gate) and the createVerificationGate/createFailureLimiter options are code-level configuration set by the process that creates the server, not request input.
security.resource_consumption: The expensive operation is scrypt (users.verifyAsync, or hashPasswordAsync with the dummy salt for unknown users), run once per well-formed, non-locked, admitted attempt on the libuv threadpool via crypto.scrypt, so it no longer blocks the event loop. Server-side bounds: the verification gate (DEC-010) lets at most 4 verifications run and at most 16 requests wait per server, and answers any further login request 503 at once without hashing; the per-username limiter allows at most 5 failed verifications per username in any 60-second span, counting attempts in flight (locked attempts skip hashing, INV-003; a successful verification requires the correct password and does not reset the count); each limiter record holds at most 5 timestamps and a pending count of at most 4; the password is capped at 1024 characters and the body at 4096 bytes; the limiter Map is capped at 10000 tracked usernames (expired, idle records pruned first, then the oldest record evicted), the session Map at 10000 tokens (oldest evicted), and the gate queue at 16 entries, each holding one parsed body of at most 4096 bytes. There is no per-IP or rate-based global limit on attempts (RISK-001).

accepted_risks.statement: An attacker rotating usernames is not rate limited per client: total verification work is capped at 4 running and 16 waiting (DEC-010), so the server stays responsive, but a sustained flood keeps the gate full and legitimate logins then get 503 until it subsides; a queued request whose client disconnected still runs its verification. No per-IP or rate-based limit is added (NG-003). Accepted because the service is a local toy with an in-memory fake user store of synthetic users, and the request defines only the per-username failure limit and the concurrency bound. Premise source: README.md ("A tiny dependency-free Node HTTP service used to exercise the gated pipeline", "a local in-memory fake user store" of synthetic users); the repo has no threat-model or accepted-risk document (.claude/pipeline.yaml security.docs is []).

Flooding more than 10000 distinct usernames inside one window evicts the oldest limiter records, which can end a lockout early. Accepted as the price of a hard memory bound on a local toy service (README.md; no repo security docs exist).

Anyone can lock a known username (for example alice) out by sending 5 wrong passwords; the lock lasts until the oldest of those failures is 60 seconds old, and an attacker who sends one more wrong password each time it lifts keeps the username locked. This is inherent in the requested per-username rule (SRC-004); the repo has no security docs that would require otherwise.

The dummy scrypt for unknown users (DEC-004) removes the gross timing difference but residual timing differences between the unknown-user and wrong-password paths (one Map lookup, timingSafeEqual) remain measurable in principle; src/users.js verifyAsync, like verify, resolves false before hashing for a missing user, and changing that behaviour is out of scope (NG-004).

Tokens never expire and are lost on restart or evicted at the 10000-session cap; since no endpoint accepts them yet (NG-001) this has no authorization effect; the store is in-memory by design (README.md).

Because attempts in verification count toward the lock (DEC-003), a correct-password attempt can get 429 with Retry-After 1 while counted failures plus in-flight attempts for its username reach 5, even if some of those in-flight attempts would succeed. This only happens when attempts for one username overlap (at most 4 can be in verification) and lasts about one scrypt duration; it is the price of keeping concurrent guesses within the requested 5 failures per 60 seconds (SRC-004). The repo has no security docs that would require otherwise (README.md: local toy service).

requirements.statement: POST /login with a JSON body {username, password} holding a registered user's correct password returns 200 with content-type application/json and body {"token": <43-character base64url string from 32 random bytes>}; each successful login issues a new distinct token, and the session store passed as options.sessions maps that token to the username. The session store holds at most 10000 tokens (MAX_TRACKED): issuing a token when it holds 10000 first evicts the oldest-issued token (INV-004, DEC-002).

acceptance.given: a server from createServer({ users: createUserStore(USERS), sessions }) listening via listen(), with the fixture users alice and bob
acceptance.when: the client POSTs {"username":"alice","password":"alice-synthetic-pw-1"} to /login twice
acceptance.then: both responses are 200 with content-type application/json, each body has exactly the key token matching /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{43}$/, and the two tokens differ

negative_control.description: Constant tokens must be caught by the distinctness assertion.
negative_control.mutation: In src/login.js, make the session store issue the fixed string "a".repeat(43) instead of crypto.randomBytes(32).toString("base64url").

acceptance.given: the same server with an injected session store
acceptance.when: alice and then bob log in with their correct passwords
acceptance.then: sessions.usernameFor(aliceToken) is "alice", sessions.usernameFor(bobToken) is "bob", and sessions.usernameFor of an unissued 43-character string is null

negative_control.description: A token that is returned but not recorded server-side must fail the readback.
negative_control.mutation: In src/login.js, return the generated token from issue() without inserting it into the session Map.

acceptance.given: a session store from createSessionStore() imported from src/login.js
acceptance.when: the test calls issue("alice") 10001 times, keeping every returned token
acceptance.then: size() is 10000, usernameFor(first token) is null, and usernameFor of the second and of the last token is "alice"

requirements.statement: Per exact username (registered or unknown), once 5 failed (401) attempts have been counted within the last 60 seconds, or counted failures plus attempts for that username currently in verification reach 5, every further attempt for that username, even with the correct password, returns 429 {"error": "too many attempts"} with a Retry-After header in whole seconds, without verifying the password (no users.verifyAsync or hashPasswordAsync call) and without counting; the lock is tested on arrival and again when a queued attempt gets its verification slot. As soon as the oldest of those 5 failures is 60 seconds old, attempts for that username are processed normally again (sliding window, DEC-003), so no 60-second span holds more than 5 401 responses for one username, even under concurrent requests. Other usernames are unaffected, and a successful login does not reset the username's failure count. The limiter tracks at most 10000 usernames (MAX_TRACKED): adding a new username when 10000 are tracked first prunes expired, idle records and then evicts the earliest-created record, so it never tracks more than 10000 (INV-004; eviction can end a lockout early, RISK-002).

requirements.statement: Password verification for POST /login runs asynchronously (users.verifyAsync, or hashPasswordAsync with the dummy salt for an unknown username, both computing the same scrypt as the synchronous functions, DEC-011) and only inside the per-server verification gate (DEC-010): at most 4 verifications run at the same time and at most 16 further well-formed, non-locked requests wait in FIFO order. A request that finds 4 running and 16 waiting gets, without any verification, 503 with content-type application/json, a retry-after: 1 header and the body {"error":"invalid credentials"} byte-identical to the 401 body, and does not count as a failed attempt for its username. A slot is freed when its verification resolves or rejects and the oldest waiting request then starts; a rejected verification answers 500 {"error": "internal error"} and does not count.
